articles.headline: Xbox boss announces Wolfenstein 3 and confirms new game in development at idSoftware despite reported job cut "bloodbath"
keyFacts: Xbox boss Asha Sharma announced that Wolfenstein 3 is in production at MachineGames and confirmed that idSoftware is working on a new game.
The announcements follow widespread Xbox restructuring and job cuts earlier this year that affected idSoftware and other studios.
Xbox has faced ongoing negative news and controversies during its 25th-anniversary year while attempting to reassure fans about upcoming franchises.
body: Xbox boss Asha Sharma has confirmed Wolfenstein 3 is in development at MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the acclaimed Wolfenstein: The New Order, Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossal, and 2024's celebrated Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. Additionally, she revealed idSoftware - one of the Microsoft-owned studio heavily impacted by sweeping Xbox job cuts earlier this year - is now working on a new game.

Sharma has, of course, been on a bit of a PR offensive of late, positioning herself alongside snippets of positive news at a time Xbox is embroiled in a massive business "reset" effort that has resulted in proposed studio closures and mass layoffs that will ultimately see 3,200 Xbox employees lose their jobs. This week's Wolfenstein 3 reveal similarly arrived in the form of a tweet posted directly from her social media account.

"Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at MachineGames," Sharma wrote on X. "One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more." As for idSoftware's new project, confirmation of that - again attributed directly to Sharma - appeared in a post on Bethesda's website. "Slaughter Mode comes to Doom: The Dark Ages - Revelations on Monday," she wrote, "and the team is already working on its next game."

In July, sweeping job cuts at Xbox resulted in 96 of idSoftware's 136 employees being laid off in a move one former team member described as a "bloodbath". Since then, idSoftware co-studio director Marty Stratton has attempted to downplay the cuts, recently insisting the studio was "doing great". He added id was "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames - a studio which appears to have escaped Sharma's restructuring efforts.

This week's Wolfenstein and idSoftware news follows similar efforts by Xbox to reassure fans their favourite franchises are unaffected by the recent layoffs. Shortly after substantial job cuts at Bethesda were confirmed, the company moved to insist The Elder Scrolls 6 was still "on the way" and that its plans were "unaffected" (the company has since released a trailer announcing its subtitle). It also confirmed a new Fallout game was in development.

Xbox's year of bad news - which includes ongoing boycott efforts relating to Microsoft's controversial involvement with the Israeli military - comes as the division celebrates its 25th anniversary. Earlier this week, Sharma shared a memo to staff marking the occasion, albeit one in which she seemingly championed a gen-AI future for games development, enthusing that, "A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers".

articles.headline: Can Man United afford Mauricio Pochettino? Compensation info as Premier League strugglers eye USMNT boss
keyFacts: Manchester United confirmed a deal to appoint Mauricio Pochettino after sacking Michael Carrick, following one win in ten league matches.
According to The Athletic, Pochettino's release clause from the United States men's national team is in the region of $10 million.
The Athletic estimated Manchester United's overall debt stands at £779 million, but the club can afford Pochettino's required compensation payments.
body: Mauricio Pochettino is the man tasked with fixing Manchester United's latest crisis.

Red Devils boss Michael Carrick was given the sack earlier this week, with United spending the November international break in the relegation zone after one win out of 10 in the Premier League this season.

Former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe and ex-Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann were the names in the frame when speculation over Carrick's future gathered pace in the aftermath of a dispiriting 3-0 loss to Bournemouth.

Since Sunday's crazy 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, several reports in the UK identified Pochettino as being among the frontrunners, as United CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox prepare for talks with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco this week. On Friday, the deal was confirmed.
It is not the first time Pochettino has been touted as a potential United manager, having been linked when Jose Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer departed in 2018 and 2021 respectively.
This time, Pochettino is settled in his job in charge of the United States men's national team and recently signed a new contract after a solid performance at the World Cup.
MORE: Ranking 5 best candidates to manage Man United
Next Man United manager: What is Mauricio Pochettino's USMNT release clause?
According to The Athletic, Pochettino's release clause from his role as head coach of the U.S. men's national team is in the region of $10 million.
Further compensation is required if United were to buy out Pochettino's coaching staff, including his longtime assistant, Jesus Perez.
After leading the United States to the Round of 16 at the World Cup, where they were beaten 4-1 by Belgium, Pochettino signed an extended contract that runs through the 2030 World Cup.

By way of comparison, numerous reports at the end of October claimed Newcastle United would be entitled to £3 million ($3.94 million) in compensation if United appointed Howe, who still had time remaining on his contract at St James' Park when he stepped down earlier this year.
Can Man United afford Pochettino?

Fans have made scathing and sustained criticisms of the Manchester United ownership during the sharp downturn in form. Carrick has been spared much criticism, while much anger has been directed towards both Ratcliffe and the Glazer family.

The Glazers' leveraged buyout of United in May 2005 cloaks all that has gone wrong on the field afterwards. A report by The Athletic earlier this month detailing United's use of revolving credit facilities (RCFs) since late 2020, estimated the club's overall debt stands at £779m.

It's part of a complicated picture for a club where revenues are projected to his record levels of between £740m and £760m this season. A return to the Champions League is a key factor here, and it already looks unlikely that United will be able to reach Europe's top competition next term.

That will have a knock-on effect, and Ratcliffe has overseen swinging off-field cuts in a vain attempt to balance the books. Major soccer clubs operating in debt, especially ones that have a significant turnover, is not uncommon and does not contravene financial rules in itself.
United could definitely afford the Pochettino compensation payments, which they've now acted on, but it is not an outlay that they can put down mindlessly.

articles.headline: Mauricio Pochettino will leave USMNT for Manchester United after Haiti matches
keyFacts: Mauricio Pochettino will officially leave the USMNT to join Manchester United after the current team camp concludes.
Pochettino served as USMNT head coach for two years, guiding the team to the World Cup round of 16.
Pochettino will coach the USMNT against Haiti in a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal before departing.
body: Mauricio Pochettino's will officially join Manchester United after the current United States men's national team camp concludes, following two years in charge of the team, including the 2026 World Cup on home soil.

For the USMNT, the timing is awkward. Though the next World Cup is still four years away, Pochettino signed a new four-year deal in August and is currently with the team at U.S. Soccer's national training center in the suburbs of Atlanta and led Wednesday's training session. The USMNT are preparing for the two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti, the first of which will take place on Saturday at Miami's Nu Stadium while the second will be on Tuesday at Cincinnati's TQL Stadium.
Defender Antonee Robinson addressed the reports on Tuesday, admitting that this is not the first time the players have been put in this situation during Pochettino's tenure.

"That news kind of got sprung on us, like the rest of the world, I'd say," Robinson said. "Similar things happened in the past, happened at the World Cup where huge teams lose their manager and they start looking at possible candidates and for us to have a manager who's linked with those sorts of jobs means we're very lucky to work with a top-level manager but it never seems to leak into the work we do, whether it's the World Cup or whether it's going to be this camp."

Pochettino was the first USMNT head coach with genuine international appeal, U.S. Soccer more often than not picking from a domestic talent pool in the team's modern history. His tenure has reflected just that – he became the federation's highest-paid coach ever when he initially joined in 2024, the salary and the scope of his role only increasing in his recent contract extension. U.S. Soccer surprisingly plucked him out of the European club game, where he had spent the entirety of his coaching career beforehand, making a name for himself at Tottenham Hotspur before later stops at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. Naturally, clubs of that ilk never lost interest and over the course of his time with the USMNT, he was linked to a handful of jobs. The most notable approach came from AC Milan, who were considering the move in the build-up to the World Cup but ultimately hired ex-Manchester United coach Ruben Amorim instead.

"Even when we first met a couple summers ago, there were lots of other people interested in having Mauricio and team join," U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson said in May. "He had standing offers from other places to come. He wanted to be here. He's a big believer in what we're doing at U.S. Soccer. He's a big believer in soccer in America and he's a big believer in this men's team and so, throughout this entire process, when you have top-class talent, whether it's salespeople, whether it's marketing people or whether it's coaches, other organizations want them and throughout this, Mauricio and team have been incredibly transparent. They've been great partners and are, of course, excited about the summer … There's been a longer list of outreach than what has even been reported and so they've been great about that."
Pochettino has also been open about his desire to return to the Premier League during his stint with the USMNT, something the move to United will accomplish.
United are currently in the relegation zone with one win in 10 games, the least of any team in the Premier League this season.
Where does Pochettino leave the USMNT?

Pochettino's track record with the USMNT is not exactly notable – he has 21 wins in 45 games, nearly all of them against teams below them in the FIFA rankings. They stumbled in a variety of ways when they attempted to punch above their weight, most notably in the World Cup round of 16 loss to Belgium that was tinged by the Folarin Balogun affair. His attempts to lead the USMNT to a statement-making run at a World Cup on home soil were mixed at best, since the team could not pass the last 16 hurdle they have been stuck at since 2010, but Pochettino still found a way to recalibrate the U.S. team in his two years in charge.

The specifics of the round of 16 elimination were a surprise, even if the exit was not. The U.S. team's player pool, talented as it was at the World Cup, was not considered amongst the world's elites so a genuinely deep run over the summer felt improbable. Pochettino, though, managed to get the best out of the group and had the USMNT playing in a way it rarely had previously – in an entertaining, high-intensity, attack-minded system. The style is a hallmark of Pochettino's coaching career but has been historically difficult to integrate at the international level, with teams usually gathering for 10 days at a time, weeks or months apart, and has historically not been the USMNT's strategy. Pochettino's predecessor Gregg Berhalter, for example, was more reserved in his tactical approach and before him, the U.S. team were known more for grit than style.

Slowly but surely, Pochettino's approach worked with the generation of players Berhalter brought in. He correctly identified that the player pool's strengths were in attack, forwards Balogun and Christian Pulisic continuing to serve as central figures for the team. More notably, though, Pochettino found use for players Berhalter had previously cast aside – midfielder Malik Tillman became a key player, his versatility something Pochettino counted as an asset. Forward Ricardo Pepi also rose up the ranks in the build-up to the World Cup, his first after being one of the last omissions from Berhalter's 2022 team.

Pochettino's legacy might actually be the player pool shakeup he oversaw on the road to the World Cup, which felt rushed because of the short timeline but was ultimately useful. Defender Alex Freeman was the breakout of the Pochettino years, going from relative obscurity at Orlando City to a World Cup starter and goalscorer in less than 500 days. Midfielder Sebastian Berhalter, the son of Pochettino's predecessor, was not on the national team's radar until his first call-up in 2025 and looks like a national team fixture for years to come. The player pool expansion project will only get more exciting from here with the USMNT's up-and-comers, with some like Cavan Sullivan and Adri Mehmeti poised to be some of the best players in the history of the men's program.

The coach's departure will sting in some ways, but his tenure ensured that the USMNT would be in a position of strength, which was hardly the case when he arrived. He inherited a team that had lost its way after a group stage exit in the Copa America and will leave behind a team with a clear enough roadmap to the 2030 World Cup. The Pochettino years prove that the next head coach should primarily be a strong tactical fit, no matter the candidate's global appeal, because he was right to identify that an attack-minded approach would suit the player pool. That's especially true with the up-and-comers since many of the brightest prospects are attackers.

There is no reason U.S. Soccer should not hire the best fit for the job but for perhaps the first time in the program's history, the USMNT's prospects might truly rest with the players at their disposal. Pochettino's successor will be chiefly tasked with getting the best out of them, much as he did with the U.S. team's core. As an exciting generation of talent finds their footing with the senior team, that's exactly how it should be.

articles.headline: ‘The will to win’: Chiefs coach explains how Travis Kelce remains dominant
keyFacts: Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy praised tight end Travis Kelce for his continued leadership and drive to win.
Kelce leads the 6-2 Chiefs in receiving with 33 catches for 482 yards in his 14th season.
Bieniemy stated that Kelce's will to win is more important to him than his individual numbers.
body: [US, Mexico & Canada customers only] Sep 5, 2025; Sao Paulo, BRAZIL; Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce (87) looks dejected after a NFL game against the Los Angeles Chargers at Corinthians Arena. Mandatory Credit: Jean Carniel/Reuters via Imagn Images Travis Kelce isn’t slowing down in his 14th season with the Kansas City Chiefs. And his offensive coordinator has a pretty simple explanation for why.

Kansas City offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy praised the 37-year-old tight end on Thursday, saying Kelce still brings the same energy and same desire to win that he did early in his career, even if his body isn’t the same.
Kelce’s Season

Kelce flirted with retirement this offseason before signaling his return , saying he was excited to see Bieniemy “back in the building.” Bieniemy returned to Kansas City as offensive coordinator, a role he held from 2018 through 2022.
Nick Wright has suggested that Taylor Swift played a big role in Kelce’s decision to come back. Either way, the decision is paying off for the 6-2 Chiefs.

Kelce has 33 catches for 482 yards this season, putting him on pace for a 1,000-yard season. He is also averaging a career-high 14.6 yards per reception, and he leads the Chiefs in receiving even after the team traded for wide receiver Josh Downs.
Not everyone has been impressed, though. Former Patriots tight end Christian Fauria recently called Kelce “soft” for his lack of willingness to block.
‘Kelce wants to win’
Bieniemy was asked on Thursday about Kelce’s continued production. He said Kelce’s drive hasn’t changed.

“The will to win, the will to want to be successful,” Bieniemy said, via KMBC . “He’s still one of those guys who brings a tremendous amount of energy. He’s a leader. He’s always providing leadership lessons to our younger players.”
Bieniemy also recalled how Kelce worked to improve his hands early in his career, catching around 200 extra passes a day during training camp.
“I mean, Kelce wants to win. I think that’s more important than anything because — and it’s not just about the numbers. He wants to help out in any way that he can,” Bieniemy said.
While Kelce is still a strong contributor on the field, Bieniemy made it clear that Kelce is valuable off the field, as well.

“I’m not shocked that he’s leading us,” Bieniemy said. “But the thing that I appreciate is all the other things that he brings to the table as far as being a leader and being a person of example of what it looks like to be a consistent professional in his business.”
At 37, Kelce is still proving that he has plenty left in the tank.

articles.headline: What we know about the global Microsoft outage
keyFacts: Microsoft attributed a major global outage affecting services like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot to elevated load on its infrastructure.
The outage disrupted operations for global users, businesses, governments, healthcare networks, and tech companies such as OpenAI.
Microsoft reported early signs of stabilization on Friday morning, but warned that some intermittent issues may continue.
body: - Published
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products.
Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
What happened?
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
How many people have been affected?
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.
The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.
The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
What has Microsoft said?
Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.
The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.
In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.
On Friday morning, Microsoft said it was seeing "early signs of stabilisation" and had made "progress" towards restoring its platforms but warned "some intermittent issues may continue".
In an earlier statement, the tech giant had said that its attempted fixes were "not taking as expected".
What have experts said?
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Paul Spain from New Zealand-based advisory firm Gorilla Technology said that with e-mails and services offline, companies have practically "lost a business day", which is "frustrating" users".

articles.headline: How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd
keyFacts: Mauricio Pochettino was named Manchester United manager on Friday, bringing a long-standing admiration for former boss Sir Alex Ferguson to the role.
Pochettino's tactical approach combines high-intensity pressing and vertical football with fluid player movement and small-space passing combinations.
Pochettino aims to succeed where Michael Carrick failed by providing better organization to a free-style approach and empowering attacking players.
body: - Published
When Mauricio Pochettino was asked the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for, he was unequivocal.
"Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson," replied Pochettino, who on Friday was named Manchester United manager.
In 2023, the Argentine - then at Chelsea, and dressed in full Blues training gear - was being interviewed by Sky Sports. Still he felt a need to express his adoration for Ferguson.
Six years prior to that interview, while managing Tottenham, he had shared lunch with the legendary former United manager.
"When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference," Pochettino said.
"And when you can share two hours with a person who was the greatest manager in the history of football, you can only enjoy."
Hiring United managers has been complicated since Ferguson's departure in 2013, and one of the most prominent complications has been a back-and-forth around the club's DNA.
For some, winning by any means necessary should take precedence, while others believe the style of play and cultural heritage of United's most successful period is vital to the club's identity.
In recent years, United's managerial merry-go-round has alternated between European coaches with their own fixed styles of play, and former players from the Ferguson era.
But between his tactics of choice and his adoration for the former United boss, Pochettino may be uniquely placed to bridge the gap between both camps.

Michael Carrick's United produced a series of good results to finish last season with a run unmatched by any other team in the league. They looked great, but it was a greatness built on attacking in a transition-heavy manner.
Under Carrick, in games they had less than 50% of the ball, they only lost once. In those 13 games, they boasted a win-rate of 62%. This dropped to 36% in games they had the majority of possession.
This style of play suited their direct attackers and protected their defenders.
At the same time, Casemiro's set-piece prowess provided United a reliable way to break the deadlock against deep defences - something they have struggled with this season.
With United a goal up, opponents stepped forward, giving Carrick's men more space. They could play to their strengths again, attacking quickly. It worked.

But teams at the top are reluctant to play in this way. Carrick's vision for United was a side that played slick football, with short passes in build-up intuitively, referencing Paris St-Germain's midfield three as a source of inspiration.
Building up in this manner, to entice and escape from pressure, before looking to find the forwards quickly, was the plan Carrick was working towards.

This didn't come to fruition and trying to take United from a successful counter-attacking side to one that could reliably beat teams while keeping the ball was the same hurdle that undid Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Erik ten Hag.
Pochettino gives United an interesting solution to this problem.

In his own words, he has described his sides as needing "to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic". He refers to himself as a "disciple" of the legendary Argentina boss Marcelo Bielsa, who he played for.

If you wanted an immediate comparison in the Premier League to a coach who resembles Pochettino's ideas in possession, it would be worth looking at Liverpool's Andoni Iraola, who similarly cites Bielsa as his reference.

These are coaches who, while taking the initiative, encourage vertical football. For as different as the clubs are, both the fans of United and Liverpool have enjoyed success when their teams have played high-octane football.
This summer's World Cup was a strong showcase of Pochettino's style of play and his recent tactical adaptation.
Rather than a fixed, positional style of play - akin to the work of somebody like Manchester City's Enzo Maresca - Pochettino's USA had only certain players being tasked with holding their position.
This approach posed problems for teams who defended in a zonal manner - defending specific areas rather than individual players.

The US midfielders being able to move freely meant they could step into areas of the pitch between the zones that were being defended, which resulted in their players often being unmarked with time and space on the ball.
By playing in close proximity to each other in the middle of the pitch, the US found another benefit.

Small-space passing combinations helped draw the opposing team up towards the ball and combined with clever off-ball movement to stretch the pitch, allowed the US to find their striker with few defenders around him.
Pochettino's men looked to thread through-balls in behind and early after enticing the opposition's press and the speedy Folarin Balogun was able to turn those chances into goals.
1 of 2
This combination of a fluid midfield, small-space passing and direct through-balls doesn't sound dissimilar to what Carrick was trying to move towards implementing this season.
And although that may worry United fans, the similarity in principles will benefit the players.
"My philosophy is to give a freer style with a good organisation," were Pochettino's words in 2014.
Although philosophically similar, that latter part - a clearer organisation to his freer style - is likely to be what Carrick was unable to reliably offer his players.

For fans of top sides, fast-paced, vertical football tends to be accepted when it comes from a place of being proactive - think Ferguson's United or Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool - wanting to keep the ball, but not passing it for passing's sake.
Fast-paced, vertical football tends to be frowned upon when it comes from a place of conceding possession and defending your own goal for long periods of the match.

The first half of Carrick's stint did appear proactive, while his 4-2-4 press worked well. Leaving four players high was a risk that allowed them to win the ball back and score quickly, but as teams figured this out, United failed to adapt.

There also appeared to be a drop in the team's fitness the longer United went from the departure of ex-boss Ruben Amorim, who left United well conditioned, albeit on the back of a schedule without European football.
Hiring Pochettino will immediately begin the process of turning United into a well-drilled side, capable of applying intense pressure, likely in a co-ordinated manner.
Pochettino enjoyed relative success with Spurs, built on this intensity and co-ordination, that differentiated him from the rest of the league.
With that unique selling point more common now than a decade ago, how he builds on it will dictate how his tenure unfolds.

But watching Brighton this season, he can be assured that an approach founded on intensity off the ball can work in the Premier League in 2026, with Fabian Hurzeler's men second in the league, with the fourth highest average possession, 10 games in.

Pochettino, from a footballing point of view, feels extremely aligned to the values of Ferguson's United, and as a result will implement numerous similarities to the things Carrick wanted, but ultimately failed, to deliver.

His wealth of experience make him a more proven entity than the departing United manager and if he can get his team fit and pressing high, in typically Pochettino fashion, they should see an upturn in form.
Expanding on his managerial approach, while managing Spurs he explained how "the most important thing [was] to create a good shape for players to be comfortable and to show their real qualities".
Rather than relying on pre-defined pattern, he looks to empower individuals to solve attacking problems. Taking this approach means recruitment of top talent matters more than ever.

"He [gave] me the confidence and licence to go where I wanted on the pitch, where I [could] use my strengths," said Cole Palmer, who enjoyed his most productive Premier League season under Pochettino at Chelsea.
United have good attackers but they will need to take the same initiative Palmer did, if platformed to their strengths - something Pochettino does well.
If they don't, and if Pochettino is to stumble, it will likely be in United's inability to break down stubborn defences when asked to dominate the ball - in what would feel like Groundhog Day, again.

body: Jake Paul’s Christmas Eve comeback card will see Mikaela Mayer and Chantelle Cameron meet again in a blockbuster sequel.
Paul will make his return to the ring against PFL star and former kickboxing champion Cedric Doumbe on December 24 in Dubai.
Paul returns against Doumbe in what will now be a stacked night to round off 2027 Getty
The influencer-turned-boxer is hoping to draw huge eyes to the event over the festive period.
UFC icon Alistair Overeem has already had his boxing debut announced on the bill against British UFC veteran Jimin Manuwa.
Cameron vs Mayer 2 added to Jake Paul card
But now, fans will be even more delighted to see a duel between two of female boxing’s pound-for-pound elite land on the card.
Cameron and Mayer, boxing’s number two and three in the rankings, will meet for the former’s unified WBO, WBA, and WBC 154lbs world titles.
It will be their second meeting, with Cameron having won their maiden clash in August with a scintillating display.
Mayer, a three-weight champion, felt aggrieved with the decision, and is gunning for revenge in their second duel.
She said: “Mayer vs. Cameron was a great fight that I truly hope everyone enjoyed.
“Although I don’t feel I performed to my highest potential, I’ve been working hard to fix the mistakes I made and I will 100% come back stronger! I’m taking my belts back on December 24.”
Cameron added: “I am genuinely excited to box in one of my favourite places on December 24 in Dubai.
“We agreed to the rematch before the first fight, so we both kept our word, and now the rematch is on the biggest stage in boxing.”
Cameron and Mayer will meet again, six months on from their captivating first outing Getty

articles.headline: Huge GOP election losses spur debates about populist economics
keyFacts: Following decisive midterm losses, Republicans are debating whether the party should abandon Donald Trump's populist economic policies and tariffs.
Former Vice President Mike Pence argued voters rejected economic populism, while Vice President JD Vance blamed foreign conflict and living costs.
Strategists predict the debate over Republican economic policy and tariffs will prominently shape the 2028 presidential primary race.
body: Top Republicans have joined a battle over the populism that the Republican Party has embraced under President Donald Trump following Democrats’ overwhelming midterm victory.

The party’s decisive disadvantage on the economy has created an opening for some conservatives, including presumed challengers to Vice President JD Vance for the GOP nomination in 2028, to call for a return to pre-Trump Republican orthodoxy, when tariffs and other populist economic policies were generally disfavored by the GOP.

“I think we’re going to have a debate about Republican economic policy for the first time in a decade,” Alex Conant, a Republican strategist and a partner at Firehouse Strategies, told the Washington Examiner .

Many voters punished Republicans for the state of the economy, which has been buffeted by higher inflation and spiking gas prices. Some two-thirds of voters in the midterm elections said that Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions , according to an Associated Press poll.
Some conservatives argued that the results were a repudiation of Trump’s populist economic agenda.
(Washington Examiner Art/Getty Images)
Marc Short, chairman of Advancing American Freedom and former chief of staff to Vice President Mike Pence, said that it is time for Republicans to “do some soul searching.”

“This happened in 2006,” Short said on X. “We regrouped and came back in 2010. Why? Because we returned to our roots of promising limited government, free markets – the things that voters wanted. Right now – GOP sounds too much like Democrats when it comes to the economy. So many of these are things that [Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)] applauds.”

But populists were quick to brush aside the notion that populism and tariffs drove voters away from Republicans. Most notably, Vance wrote a lengthy post placing the blame on discontent with the war with Iran, the U.S. relationship with Israel, and a lack of focus on cost-of-living issues from the GOP.
Vance didn’t mention tariffs or populism at all in the post.
On the other side, Pence wrote in the Wall Street Journal that the midterm results showed that voters “rejected our party’s shift toward economic populism,” and specifically mentioned tariffs.

“As we saw Tuesday night, many Americans will still vote conservative, but some will stay home,” Pence wrote. “Worse yet, some will become so repulsed by populism and corruption that they will vote for the other side.”
Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL), a possible 2028 contender, blasted the outcome as an “extinction-level event for Republicans” and pointed out that Republicans did better in his state of Florida.
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), who is seen as closer to the traditional free-market side of the party, wasn’t shy about mentioning tariffs.
“Tariffs have made everything too expensive and the Iran war has dragged on too long,” Cruz said on his podcast.

Conant predicted that this debate will most prominently play out within the GOP in the lead-up to the 2028 presidential election, during the primary process. He said the race might be much more competitive now given this week’s results.
Jason Roe, a veteran Republican political consultant, told the Washington Examiner that he thinks tariffs, in particular, will be a focus in 2028.
“As we talk about what you know the Republican coalition looks like moving into the future, I think it’s very much going to be one of the top three or four issues that we are debating,” Roe said.
Exit polling showed that 66% of voters said that Trump’s tariff policies have hurt the economy. Just 21% said that tariffs have provided a boost for the economy.

Some on the populist Right have pointed to the higher gas prices resulting from the war in Iran as the reason why people were dissatisfied with Republicans and voted for Democrats. But the polling shows those policies aren’t popular.
“One of the things underreported, I think, so far is it seems from exit polls that tariffs were a big driver for the vote against Republicans,” Roe added.

And the GOP can’t blame Trump alone for the tariffs. Republicans in the House worked to safeguard Trump’s tariffs and prevent Congress from batting them down. They took unusual procedural steps to disable Democrats’ ability to force votes on tariffs.

In April of last year, after the announcement of Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs, GOP leaders inserted language into unrelated legislation that prevented members from circumventing leadership and voting to rescind the tariffs.

Then, in September 2025, the GOP House Rules Committee further extended the blockade until earlier this year. But then in February, Reps. Kevin Kiley (I-CA), Thomas Massie (R-KY), and Don Bacon (R-NE) broke with the party and joined Democrats to sink a procedural vote that would have extended it further.
Still, some Republicans support Trump’s tariff agenda as a way to reshore manufacturing.

Nick Iacovella, executive vice president at the pro-tariff Coalition for a Prosperous America, told the Washington Examiner that he thinks populism will remain a “permanent fixture” of the Republican Party.

“To think that these guys are going to say that we’re going to go back to globalism and free trade, they’re not reading the tea leaves properly, and they’re not going to win an election,” Iacovella said.

He also drew the distinction between different types of tariffs. For instance, Iacovella said some tariffs targeting specific products, such as the Section 232 tariffs, have been more successful and popular than some retaliatory tariffs, such as those targeting Canada.
Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 gives the president broad power to levy tariffs when there is a threat to national security.
“Our advice to the administration has always been: use tariffs to either raise revenue or to reshore industry,” Iacovella said.
Still, some on the Right think that the debate over populism will land the party back closer to where it was before Trump and others transformed the GOP.

Brian Darling, a Republican strategist and former Senate aide, told the Washington Examiner that tariffs were a “huge issue” in the midterm elections, and that the scale of Democrats’ gains could force Republicans to reassess and return to more traditional views.

“I do think the Republican Party will shift towards more of a free market view, the traditional view of the Republican Party with low tariffs or no tariffs, and a view to getting inflation under control by using market forces instead of using government power,” Darling said.
DEMOCRATS PLAN TO USE MAJORITIES TO FORCE GOP TO TAKE TOUGH VOTES ON TRUMP TARIFFS
But the elephant in the room is Trump.

“Frankly, the Republican primary is going to look very much like the reality show The Apprentice , with Trump kind of lording over the contestants and probably inserting himself here and there,” Roe said.
Zach Halaschak ( @zhalaschak ) is the economics reporter for the Washington Examiner , based in Washington, D.C.

articles.headline: Rocket Report: Starship set for historic test flight; a century of Electron
keyFacts: SpaceX plans a Friday Starship launch to attempt the full recovery of its upper stage on Saturday.
Rocket Lab is scheduled to launch its 100th Electron rocket mission from New Zealand on November 14.
Italian rocket builder Avio outlined required investment to increase the annual launch cadence of its Vega C rocket.
body: Welcome to Edition 9.19 of the Rocket Report! Will something historic happen this weekend? No orbital rocket has ever been fully recovered with the intent of reusing all of its components. But that’s just what SpaceX is going to try to do with a Starship launch on Friday, and an upper stage landing attempt 22.5 hours later on Saturday afternoon, local time. Ars will be on hand in Starbase, Texas, to provide coverage of it all.

As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

Electron set for milestone launch. The next launch of Rocket Lab’s Electron vehicle is due to lift off from the Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand on November 14 at 5:30 UTC. This mission will serve as Electron’s 100th overall mission—a notable milestone for the small rocket that first flew in 2017, NASASpaceflight.com reports.

A true commercial success … This flight of Electron, named “The Mountain God Rises,” will deliver another iQPS satellite into LEO for iQPS’s synthetic aperture radar constellation. The anniversary rocket features a special gold-and-black livery which looks fantastic. Rocket Lab truly does deserve recognition as the world’s second purely commercial launch business to make a successful go at it. We are all celebrating with them.

Is the Vega rocket a dead end? Last month, Italian rocket builder Avio presented a market update that outlined the additional investment required to increase the annual launch cadence of its Vega C rocket to six and eventually nine flights per year, European Spaceflight reports. The need for this additional funding raises an interesting question about the future of Italy’s Vega launch vehicle family. Is investing in the infrastructure needed to secure just three more Vega C flights per year by the end of the decade the best use of resources, particularly when several emerging European launch companies appear poised to offer comparable capacity?

articles.headline: Jeffries shredded over Hegseth impeachment snafu as Dem jockeys for speaker’s gavel
keyFacts: House Republicans blocked an impeachment push against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth after 11 House Democrats missed a procedural vote.
Critics questioned Hakeem Jeffries' leadership after missed votes, but strategist Mike Nellis said most Democrats still have faith in him.
Journalist David Schuster noted that the Hegseth impeachment can be reintroduced when Democrats take the House majority in January.
body: Back-to-back blunders on the House floor are raising questions over whether Democrats are ready for primetime as they're poised to take over the majority — and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., makes a bid for the top role.

Democrats are projected to win 255 House seats, with 12 races yet to be called, and Jeffries is running to be Speaker of the House following the sweeping victories last week that saw the party make gains even in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, Mississippi, Kansas and South Carolina.
But some have questioned whether the recent snafus signal that Jeffries and other leaders may not be ready to be in command of the House majority.

"I may have to rethink my support of Hakeem Jeffries after the Hegseth impeachment vote," Fred Trump III, a Democrat, author and nephew of President Donald Trump, posted on X. "Eleven Democrats do not show up? All Republicans vote it down."
" Pete Hegseth is laughing at you and is stronger today. Shame," he continued. "A slap in the face of the military and veterans on this important day."
HEGSETH THWARTS GOP-LED IMPEACHMENT PUSH AS QUESTIONS SWIRL OVER WHETHER ALLEGATIONS RISE TO HIGH CRIMES
House GOP leaders' successfully blocked Rep. Thomas Massie , R-Ky., from leading the charge to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth earlier this week.
Part of the reason for the failure was the absence of 11 House Democrats during a procedural vote on Tuesday evening.
Had just seven of them been present, the vote to kill Massie's impeachment resolution would have failed, triggering debate and a vote on impeaching the Cabinet secretary likely the next day.
"Everyone knew that attendance was key tonight but somehow Democratic leaders failed to deliver and handed Republicans a win," Demand Progress Executive Director Sean Vitka said in a statement.
'THE VIEW' CO-HOST CALLS DEMOCRATS MISSING HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE A 'SELF-INFLICTED WOUND'

Progressive journalist David Schuster wrote on X, "Sure, house Dems will have 259 seats in January instead of current 213. And Hegseth impeachment can be reintroduced. But Hakeem having 11 Dem absences today on Hegseth (thus losing vote) reveals a Hakeem leadership problem. Embarrassing."
An emotional Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said in a video posted to X that she and other Democrats were stuck in traffic when they missed the vote.
Various reports , however, said they were at a fundraiser less than two miles from the U.S. Capitol.
HOUSE DEM MISSES HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE BECAUSE OF MAJOR MEDICAL PROCEDURE ONE WEEK AFTER ELECTION DAY
Others blamed medical procedures and family emergencies.
The day after, a bill Democratic leadership was actively urging lawmakers to vote against passed by unanimous voice vote — simply because no Democrats called for a roll call instead.

Democrats accused Republicans of parliamentary tricks, including a post on the X account belonging to the House Veterans Affairs Committee minority, "Republicans pushed it through that way intentionally so their members wouldn’t have to go on the record supporting cuts to veterans’ benefits."
But the majority of Democrats do not believe it is an early blight on Jeffries' potential speakership .
HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE

"I think there's frustration in terms of whipping votes. I'm not entirely sure where the breakdown is. And it does seem like there's maybe some tension somewhere," Democratic strategist Mike Nellis told Fox News Digital. "I think it'll be incumbent on the incoming speaker to make sure that everybody feels like they're on the same page...beyond that, if you're asking me if it makes a difference in a leadership flight, I mean, nobody's running against Hakeem. I haven't heard of anybody seriously thinking about doing that, so I don't know that it'll change anything."
He said House Democrats largely "have faith" in Jeffries and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., who is poised to be the next House Majority Leader .

Democrat Dan Turrentine, co-host of "The Huddle," told Fox News Digital "a few Democrats unintentionally missed one vote. Unfortunately this happens periodically in both chambers, for both parties. It does not speak to Jeffries' leadership."
And other House Democrats, when asked, directed frustration at their colleagues instead.

"My message is always to members that we need to be here and be on time," Clark told reporters Wednesday. "But there was a clear message from the Republican Party as well that they are unwilling, even after this election, to stand up against Hegseth in this war."
Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., said, "It's unfortunate, but that's not on leadership."
Fox News Digital reached out to Jeffries' political team for comment.

articles.headline: Democrats fumbled the Hegseth impeachment. That could be a blessing in disguise | Claire Finkelstein
keyFacts: House Republicans defeated Representative Thomas Massie's articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following Democratic disorganization and traffic delays.
Claire Finkelstein argued Democrats can refocus impeachment on Hegseth's classified Signal chats, civilian boat strikes, and retribution against Senator Mark Kelly.
Leaders of the 120th Congress will have opportunities to pursue impeachment inquiries and executive oversight in the new year.
body: A traffic jam, combined with disorganization on the part of Democrats, enabled House Republicans to scuttle the representative Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.
While recriminations are now flying among Democrats, the fumble may have been a blessing in disguise. Democrats can now refocus the articles against the defense secretary, possibly to better effect.

The first four of Massie’s articles of impeachment addressed the Iran war, asserting that the Department of Defense overstepped presidential war powers authority. The first three accused Hegseth of failing to respect congressional authority and the War Powers Resolution. And the fourth claimed that that the Pentagon failed to mitigate harm to civilians in its operations, resulting in the tragedy of the US strike on the girls’ school in Minab, Iran.
Inclusion of the first four articles of impeachment, however, might ultimately have backfired in the Senate, and maybe even in the House in the final vote.

The US has a long history of presidents ignoring Congress’s role in decisions to engage in military force. From Nixon’s invasion of Laos and Cambodia, to US-led Nato intervention in Kosovo and Serbia under Bill Clinton, to US military intervention in Libya under Barack Obama, among others, presidents and their secretaries of defense have flouted Congress’s role in authorizing military operations for years.

The same can be said about harm to civilians in US operations. It was mistaken strikes against civilians during the Obama years that inspired Secretary Mattis, followed by Secretary Austin, to establish the now-shuttered Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response program. Dismantling the program was a Hegseth initiative and one of Massie’s concerns.
A more targeted set of articles in the new Congress might stand a better chance of success.

Three causes for impeachment stand out as most likely to garner bipartisan support. The first is one that did not even appear in Massie’s articles: Hegseth’s egregious handling of classified communications in the infamous Signal chat conversation regarding a planned military operation in Yemen, when the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, Jeffrey Goldberg, was inadvertently included on the thread.

“Signalgate”, as it has been called, identifies one of the worst cases of mishandling classified information ever to occur by a higher-level official in the defense department. A Pentagon report itself suggests that Hegseth put troops in danger in this incident.

Hegseth and other members of the administration continued to exchange classified information on Signal even after the initial revelation by the Atlantic. Hegseth then embarked on extensive internal investigations, using polygraph testing to search for leakers, and ultimately firing Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a member of the joint staff. Yet the secretary himself, or at least his lax practices, may well have been the source of some of the very leaks he is investigating.

Second, boat strikes directed against civilian vessels in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific stand on a different footing from the articles relating to the Iran war. This use of US military force has been virtually unanimously condemned by legal experts as an indisputable violation of the laws of war, or, more accurately, as murder.

Third, an article of impeachment addressing the vindictive campaign of retribution against the senator Mark Kelly for a controversial video he made with five other members of Congress could well garner support from Republicans, some of whom may rise to the occasion to defend their colleague.

As I made clear in a brief in support of Mark Kelly, the video, which reminded troops they may refuse to follow illegal orders, merely restated textbook training to servicemembers regarding the law of superior orders. The attack on Kelly was not popular with either Democratic or Republican members of Congress.
As I recently wrote about possible impeachment charges against Trump, Congress’s heightened investigatory powers during an impeachment inquiry provide a critical benefit of the process.

A Hegseth impeachment could force release of the Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) memo justifying the boat strikes. OLC lawyers should be called on to testify – presumably behind closed doors – to explain the process by which they came to support the strikes.
An investigation of the OLC is long overdue in any event, and a more general inquiry should be conducted by the House and Senate judiciary committees.
Hegseth’s attack on Pentagon lawyers should also be investigated and should possibly form a fourth article in newly refocused impeachment charges against him.

Starting with the firing of the top Judge Advocate Generals and moving on to incursions into the role played by rank-and-file Jags, Hegseth has sought to undermine fidelity to the rule of law and the role of lawyers in reviewing military operations.

While Congress has heard some testimony on these matters, such as that of Adm Frank Bradley, who took the hit himself for certain of the boat strikes in a likely attempt to protect Hegseth, many questions remain unanswered.
Most critically, impeachment proceedings against Hegseth will provide an opportunity for Congress to strengthen its oversight authority.

Hegseth will likely invoke either presidential “testimonial immunity” or “deliberative privilege”, doctrines made up by the executive branch over time that have rarely been tested in article III courts.

While it is true that presidents need to be able to consult with members of their cabinets confidentially without fear of public revelation, these doctrines have served more to interfere with congressional oversight and block transparency than to further sound presidential decision-making. Congress must work to cut these outsized claims of presidential authority down to size.
There will also likely be assertions that information cannot be shared with Congress due to classification concerns.

Here, too, Congress must stand firm and focus on rebuilding its oversight authority. Members of the two armed services committees have robust classification privileges that make sharing information with Congress behind closed doors entirely legal and appropriate.

Leaders of the 120th Congress will have the opportunity to lead critical impeachment inquiries as well as conduct extensive oversight in the new year, but they must play their cards carefully and keep their eyes on the prize – long-term restoration of democratic norms and the strengthening of checks and balances in the federal government.

- Claire Finkelstein, a contributing opinion writer for the Guardian, is the Algernon Biddle professor of law and professor of philosophy at the University of Pennsylvania. She is also the founder and faculty director of Penn’s Center for Ethics and the Rule of Law (CERL). She is a fellow in residence at the Edmond & Lily Safra Center for Ethics at Harvard University during the 2026-27 academic year

articles.headline: Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from USA to Manchester United confirmed
keyFacts: Mauricio Pochettino has been confirmed as the new manager of Manchester United on a two-and-a-half-year deal.
Manchester United paid about $10m to US Soccer to secure Pochettino, who will start his new role after two Concacaf matches.
Pochettino replaces Michael Carrick, who was sacked after leading Manchester United to their worst start in four decades.
body: Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.

The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades. United have won one of their past 11 games and are in the Premier League’s relegation zone.

United made Pochettino their first-choice target after it became clear Carrick would be dismissed. They only held talks with the Argentinian, despite interest in the former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann. United’s leadership group selected Pochettino over other candidates and had the decision to appoint him signed off by Sir Jim Ratcliffe this week.

The club were attracted to Pochettino based on his personality, hoping he can turn things around at United by building a strong culture within the dressing room. United sought a more experienced coach after Carrick, feeling Pochettino’s long-term record of player development and clear philosophy would suit the needs of United at the moment.

Pochettino signed a new four-year contract with US Soccer in August, an expansive deal that offered the Argentinian greater control over youth development and the overall direction of the men’s programme. To secure his services, United have paid the US federation about $10m (£7.5m), with an additional fee paid to secure the services of Pochettino’s longtime assistants.

United’s players not on international duty were told on Thursday they did not need to return to training until next week. With the second of the US’s two games against Haiti finishing in the early hours of Wednesday GMT, Pochettino’s first day with United is expected to be Thursday.

“The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honours of my career. We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country,” Pochettino said on Friday.

“We want to thank Cindy Parlow Cone, JT Batson and Dan Helfrich for their partnership and incredible working relationships throughout our time here. There is tremendous talent in the US player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of US Soccer. You will always have a special place in our hearts, and we will be supporting the teams whenever they step on the field.”

Pochettino was hired by US Soccer in September 2024, brought on to steer the US through their first home World Cup in 32 years. Over the ensuing two years he compiled a 21-12-2 record and guided the team to the World Cup last 16, results that stack up favourably alongside other US coaches.

He earned praise in the US for his enthusiasm and for putting together the US men’s greatest group stage at a World Cup, a performance that included a 4-1 dismantling of Paraguay that will go down as the team’s best 90-minute performance at the tournament. All of that early progress, though, was wiped out by a 4-1 loss to Belgium in the last 16, a result marred by the federation’s – and Pochettino’s – handling of the red card controversy surrounding US forward Folarin Balogun.

It was not his only lowlight: there was the shocking fourth-place finish in the 2024-25 Nations League and a bitterly disappointing loss to Mexico in the 2025 Gold Cup final. The US were thrashed by top-level competition in friendly matches, and Pochettino sometimes struggled to connect with players, primarily the Milan midfielder Christian Pulisic. Others, such as Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie, found themselves in and out of the picture on a regular basis.

Pochettino leaves the US with a glimmer of hope for the future. Across his tenure, 75 players earned at least one cap for the US. articles.headline: New Game from Doom studio and New Wolfenstein Announced

body: Xbox is celebrating its 25th anniversary this month, and it's been spoiling fans left and right. Xbox games like Minecraft, Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, Gears E-Day, and more received celebratory freebies. Beyond the awesome free in-game items, players were lucky enough to get a few exciting announcements coming from Bethesda-owned studios, Id Software and MachineGames.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma took to X this Thursday to discuss improvements coming to Xbox, but that's not all. Sharma promoted the launch of Slaughter mode, an endless combat mode for Doom: The Dark Ages. In this mode, gamers will fight through increasingly stronger hordes of randomly selected demons to get a higher score and collect Skulls that can be exchanged for unique rewards. After each wave, they must decide whether to continue and risk all their progress or give up and try again later.

The Slaughter Mode update for Doom: The Dark Ages is scheduled to be released on Monday, Nov. 16. It is free for players who own the Revelations DLC or those who got the premium edition or upgrade for Doom: The Dark Ages.
Id Software and MachineGames are working on new games

Doom: The Dark Ages developer Id Software responded to Sharma's post about the update and announced that its teams in Texas and Frankfurt are working on a new game. It seems like the mystery game is still in the early stages of development, as Id Software was not able to share much, but it did confirm that it will be directed by Hugo Martin, who helmed The Dark Ages.

That wasn't the only new game reveal that we got on Thursday. Sharma confirmed that Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at MachineGames. This was expected, as last year, studio head Jerk Gustafsson confirmed that the Wolfenstein reboot was always envisioned as a trilogy. However, confirmation of development is still a huge leap from mere rumors and discussion.

Both game announcements were short on details, so it's likely that they're still in the early stages of development. Nevertheless, it's great news for fans who were looking forward to more games from these studios. For now, we will have to wait to learn more, but thankfully, we have Doom: The Dark Ages' new game mode to keep us busy.

articles.headline: “You Guys Are F***ing Idiots”: Jeff Kaplan Takes Aim At Blizzard’s Overwatch 2 Reveal
keyFacts: Former Overwatch director Jeff Kaplan criticized Blizzard's 2019 reveal of Overwatch 2, stating leadership lacked a clear vision or business model.
Kaplan said he experienced constant friction with Blizzard executives from 2018 until he lost his agency and decided to leave the company in 2021.
Kaplan is currently working on The Legend of California at his new studio, Kintsugiyama.
body: Saying Overwatch 2 has had a rocky road since its 2019 reveal would be an understatement, and former Overwatch director Jeff Kaplan isn't a fan of how the game was first announced.

Speaking to Gaming World Interviews , Kaplan didn't mince words about the BlizzCon 2019 opening ceremony, where Overwatch 2 was shown for the first time, as Blizzard promised numerous features it either walked back or didn't deliver.

Kaplan said that from 2018 until his departure, he experienced constant friction with Blizzard's executive leadership over game direction, scheduling, and core game mechanics. This led him to confront leadership about the lack of a clear vision or business model for Overwatch 2, and to question the wisdom of announcing Overwatch 2 at the same time as Diablo 4.
https://youtu.be/98HNSuXHtys

"I got in a huge fight with, at the time, it wasn't Mike [Morhaime]. I loved Mike, who was the president of Blizzard, and another president of Blizzard, my executive producer, over announcing Overwatch 2. I went into their office, I’m like, 'What are we doing? We don’t really know what this game is; we don’t know what the business model is. This is a huge mistake.'"

According to Kaplan, the new executives "had a lot to prove" when they joined Blizzard. "They wanted to prove that 'Blizzard's back and Blizzard still has it.' And I'm like, 'You guys are f***ing idiots,' you know? I don’t know how else to put it, but after three years of just getting worn down and not agreeing with any of the decisions that were being made on the franchise and not feeling like I had agency anymore--like before it used to be like I'm the game director I get to decide the direction the game goes. And starting in 2018, I lost that, and after three years of fighting for it back, I realized this company belongs to these corporate people now, the Blizzard executive team, the Activision team."

Kaplan left Blizzard in 2021, saying Activision Blizzard’s financial arm told him that if Overwatch didn't meet certain financial goals, 1,000 people at the company would be laid off and the blame would fall on him. "The biggest f**k you moment I’ve had in my career--it felt surreal to be in that condition," Kaplan said earlier this year .

These days, Kaplan is working on The Legend of California at the new studio he co-founded, Kintsugiyama. The Blizzard veteran recently spoke to GameSpot about the "humbling" reality of being an indie dev and more.

articles.headline: Three-quarters of House members seeking statewide office lost
keyFacts: Twenty-one of 28 House members who ran for statewide office lost their bids in the 2026 midterm elections.
Representative John James lost Michigan's governor race to Democrat Jocelyn Benson, and Democrat Christina Hines won his House seat.
Incoming governors Marsha Blackburn and Amy Klobuchar will appoint their Senate replacements in Tennessee and Minnesota.
body: Many people who have been in the workforce for a while can think back to jobs that they stayed in too long and should have left earlier. Conversely, many people regret quitting a job they should have stayed in, usually in the hope that their next move would be an improvement, professionally and/or financially.

Rep. John James (R-MI) may fall into the electoral version of the latter category. James, in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, lost badly to Democratic nominee Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state for the past eight years, in the Wolverine State’s gubernatorial race.

Benson’s win was among a plethora of Democratic bright spots in the 2026 elections . Voters made clear their disdain for the country’s current course nearly halfway through President Donald Trump’s second term. While romping in states like Michigan, Democratic congressional candidates, too, demolished Republican opponents, winning both chambers of Congress. The incoming Democratic House majority could reach over 260 members in the 435-member chamber. And with only the Alaska Senate race uncalled, Democrats could hold up to 56 seats in the 100-member body, a stark improvement from the 53-47 GOP edge in the current Congress .

For Republicans, while they have to squint pretty hard to find any bright spots following the elections, there are a few data points available. Among them, six GOP House members won statewide office, compared to a single Democrat. Unfortunately for departing James in Michigan, he wasn’t part of the group. Rather, James was among the 21 House members who lost bids for statewide office in 2026 — Senate, governor, and state attorney general — making for a dismal 25% success rate among these politically ambitious members of Congress.
By itself, a statewide defeat need not be a political career-ender. After all, many aspiring politicians have lost statewide races and bounced back to other elected offices.

The problem for James, 45, is that the House seat he won in 2022 was itself a comeback bid after a pair of losing Senate bids. He came up short in 2018, losing about 52% to 46% to then-Sen. Debbie Stabenow, in what would turn out to be Michigan’s final race of her 24-year Senate career. In 2020, James was again the Michigan Republican Senate nominee but lost to Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI), 49.90% to 48.22%.

James rebounded in 2022 to win the open Macomb County 10th Congressional District, covering a politically diverse swath of territory north of Detroit. That would seem like a pretty good political sinecure after two statewide losses. Adding insult to injury, the seat flipped on Nov. 3. James will be succeeded by attorney Christina Hines.
Still, it’s easy to see why James would gravitate toward statewide races in Michigan, with an eye on a future run for national office.

“After graduating from the United States Military Academy in 2004, he served eight years in the Army, including as an Apache helicopter pilot during Operation Iraqi Freedom,” wrote the 2026 Almanac of American Politics . “After retiring from the military, James joined the family business, which blossomed into a global supply-chain management company. James eventually became its president.”

In other words, a political consultant’s dream: a military veteran, successful businessman, and one of four black House Republicans in the expiring 119th Congress — each will be gone starting next year due to state electoral wins, losses, or retirement. But James’s defeats in three statewide races may be the end of his statewide political ambitions.
Two departing senators will choose their replacements

Incoming governors include Sens. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) and Amy Klobuchar (D-MN). Both have time left in their current six-year Senate terms, and each will likely, as their first act as governors, appoint their successor in D.C.

Gov.-elect Blackburn was elected to the Senate in 2018 after 16 years as a House member. Tennessee voters reelected her in 2024, and her successor will get nearly two years in office before presumably seeking election in their own right for the middle two years of the six-year Senate term. That person would then likely run in the 2028 special election for the seat’s final two years in office.

Many are likely to be tapped for the Senate seat. Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) has already spoken publicly about his interest in a Senate appointment. As for Minnesota and Gov.-elect Klobuchar’s Senate appointment, the situation is the same as Tennessee. Klobuchar, first elected in 2006, won reelection in 2024.

Blackburn and Klobuchar are joined in ditching D.C. for a governorship by Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-AL). The Alabama governor-elect won a closer-than-expected victory, about 52% to 48% over former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones, whom he defeated in 2020. Since Tuberville’s six-year Senate term was already expiring, there’s no successor to appoint. Rep. Barry Moore (R-AL) won the 2026 Alabama Senate race and will soon move across the Capitol for his new gig in the upper chamber.

Governorships were among the many bright spots for Democrats in the midterm elections. The party is poised to win 30 governorships, 60% of the nation’s total. That will be the first Democratic majority of governorships since early 2010.

articles.headline: BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn
keyFacts: An IT worker and his colleague disrupted network systems and set fire to their building to stop their boss's new idea.
The worker wiped the boss's laptop and mobile phone while falsely claiming a virus was attacking the building.
The colleague later reviewed the boss's written notes and said the proposed idea was not that bad.
body: Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach...
And look, the Boss has his office door open!
C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D !

The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open.

His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us.
And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas.
"AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop.

He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town.
"For the security system," the Boss teases.
I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same.
The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea.
>clickety< >tap<
"Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed."
>tappity<
"And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too."
"It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to.
"A virus?!" the Boss gasps.
"I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing.

So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him.
Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow...
>tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety<
On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously.
>tappity< >tap<
The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight.
On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling.
>bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip<
>ring<
"Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback.
"It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!"
Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard.
"What do I do?" the Boss gasps.
"It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!"
"I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks.
DAMMIT!
>tappity< >click< >tap< >tap<
Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device...
The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan.
...two hours later...
"So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden.
"Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor."
"It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation."
"It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used."
"Really? Was it... enthusiasm?" I ask.
"No, more like lighter fluid."
"Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know."
"Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks.
"Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie.
...Later, in Mission Control...
"So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building."
"Yes."
"Simply to stop a dumb idea?"
"Yes."
"And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad."
"Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious.

articles.headline: Man dies after eating bomb disguised as traditional sweet
keyFacts: A 35-year-old man in India died after a crude bomb disguised as a sweet exploded in his mouth, police said.
Fellow villagers gave him the wild-boar hunting device, which closely resembled a traditional dessert, police and local media reported.
Police have arrested and charged two men with culpable homicide while investigating the motive behind the incident.
body: An Indian man died after a crude bomb disguised as a traditional sweet exploded in his mouth, police said Friday.

Some rural communities use the homemade devices to kill wild boars by packing balls of dough with gunpowder, often sourced from firecrackers or quarries. According to the Economic Times, the devices are designed to explode when an animal bites them.
But they also resemble a common Indian dessert called rasgulla, a soft, round sweet soaked in sugar syrup -- and traditionally eaten whole.
The dead man was identified as 35-year-old Rajendra Barautiya.
He was gathered around a bonfire on Tuesday in Dindori district, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, when a fellow villager brought the "sweet" and another gave it to him.
"The bomb, used by some tribal people in the area to kill wild boars, was offered to this man," police officer Rekha Singh told AFP. "It exploded in his mouth."
Barautiya was rushed to hospital with severe injuries but died.
The villager who handed him the sweet was identified by police as Ramabhagat Barautiya, who described it as a rasgulla, the New Indian Express reported.
"The incident has triggered widespread shock and fear in the village, with residents struggling to comprehend how a casual evening conversation ended in such a tragic manner," the outlet said.
Two men have been arrested and charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
"We don't know if the motive was to kill, or if it was a mischief," Singh added. "That is a matter of investigation."
