articles.headline: Democrats made shocking gains with religious voters — but not everywhere
keyFacts: Catholic voters swung left to narrowly back Democrats 50 to 49 percent in 2026, according to exit polls.
Exit polls indicated that evangelical Christian turnout fell, while Jewish voters shifted slightly toward the Republican Party.
Voter roll-validated studies from the Pew Research Center will be released next year to provide clearer data.
body: Voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling location inside St. Patrick Parish Center in White Lake, Michigan on Election Day. | Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images
One of the most eye-opening aspects of last week’s midterms was the new cohort of religious politicians it sent to Congress — many of them part of a wave of Democratic-leaning Christians .
Another striking feature was the dramatic shift among many religious voters.

For years, American politics has seemed stuck on a partisan track, with religious-identified voters shifting more firmly to the right, and the nonreligious tacking to the left. There are a few exceptions , of course — Jewish voters, Latino Catholics, and Black Protestants, who have stayed firmly Democratic — but the broader tide has flowed clearly one way.
Key takeaways
This year’s blue tsunami carried voters everywhere to the left; it also scrambled voting trends in America’s religious electorate.
Catholics shifted hard to the left after Donald Trump won their vote by a double-digit margin in 2024.
Jewish voters were still strongly Democratic, though there are clear signs of lower support than in previous electoral cycles.
Other religious groups, mainline Protestants and Muslims, contributed to a diverse Democratic coalition — while evangelicals appeared less enthusiastic to turn out.

The 2026 vote, for the first time in a while, makes that picture look less certain. Based on exit polls, county-level data, and some post-election analysis, we already have a handful of intriguing signs of change. The data is still early and patchy, but it appears that Catholic voters around the country moved left, evangelical Christians stayed home, and some Jewish voters dug in against the anti-Israel rhetoric and moved rightward. And in Utah, generational differences, particularly among Mormons, may be starting to change the political makeup of a rock-ribbed conservative state.

There are caveats: Wave elections, especially when they’re of the historic proportions of last week’s Democratic tsunami, can obscure and cloud these changes. When everyone moves in one direction, it can be hard to distinguish specific storylines. And with religion, as with any single voter attribute, it can be difficult to tease out just how much faith and religious identity influenced vote choice, as opposed to working in combination with race, class, and concerns about issues like affordability and immigration.
And better data is still to come; the gold standard of voter roll-validated studies , like the Pew Research Center’s , won’t be available until next year.

Yet that combination of factors also suggests a new possibility for our politics: that religious voters of all creeds can come to function as swing voters too, cracking up old alliances, like on the religious right , and offering the hint of new winning coalitions, as Catholics and mainline Protestant Christians seem to have done for the Democrats.
The largest shift: Catholic voters swung against the GOP

Catholics play a special role in American politics. They spent much of the last century operating as a solid Democratic bloc , reaching a peak in the 1960s when John F. Kennedy, the first Catholic president, won about 80 percent of their vote. Since then, they’ve gradually become more Republican, due to assimilation of former European Catholic immigrants, the rise of conservative activism over abortion and social issues, and the rise of the religious right.

In the last two decades, Catholics have tended to reflect the views of the median American voter, evenly split in the 2012, 2016, and 2020 presidential elections. But that changed in 2024. Across different polls and surveys, Catholics shifted decisively to the right: backing Trump 59-39 according to exit polls, and 55-43 , according to the Pew Research Center.

Now, in a year in which Trump and Republicans frequently clashed with Pope Leo XIV and his bishops — over the Iran war, mass deportations, and immigration policy — Catholic voters again turned into a wild card.

This year, according to exit polls , they swung left , with the margin shifting by more than 20 points. Democrats narrowly won the Catholic vote this time, 50-49. As a subgroup, that put Catholics up there with Asian voters, Latinos, urban and suburban voters, Gen Z and millennials as being the top groups that swung to the left this year.
View Link

Other estimates from the religion and politics scholar Ryan Burge show particularly noticeable shifts among white Catholics, swinging about 9 points toward Democrats, even if a majority of them still voted for Republican congressional candidates. In Texas, his analysis showed that counties with higher shares of Latino Catholics were much more likely to support the winning Democratic Senate candidate, James Talarico.

The results were even more dramatic in the most Catholic House districts. Of the 12 districts with the highest share of Catholics, the average swing in the vote was about 15 points, and Democrats won eight of these seats, while gaining in all 12.

Catholics have tended to basically operate like the median voter — swinging in the same direction as the overall popular vote. That makes it harder to pinpoint any unique motivators that caused Catholics to move against the GOP: Trump’s fights with Catholic leaders, the lack of a mobilized anti-abortion movement this year, or the affordability concerns that moved all voters.

One notable exception here are Latino Catholics, who tend to be the most Democratic of the Catholic electorate, and most opposed to Trump’s immigration and deportation policies this cycle. It’s no coincidence that they’re concentrated in the Southwest, including those parts of Texas that swung toward Talarico and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa over both economic stress and anger over immigration enforcement.

Does this all suggest the rise of a new Catholic swing vote? Potentially — combined with the decline in abortion politics in the US, and a more active Vatican. For the first time, the Church has an American pope, one who isn’t afraid to get involved with current affairs and push harder on Catholic social teachings (which align more with the Democratic Party’s views of society and the economy). That could have meaningful repercussions heading into 2028.
Though still very blue, some Jewish voters broke with the Democrats

Jewish Americans, though they only make up about 2 percent of the American population, became a huge focus of political attention this year — in large part because of how central they are to Democratic coalitions (along with Black Americans, they are some of the most loyal Democratic voters), and because Israel became a flashpoint in American politics.

As Democrats made a dramatic shift in the last two years in how they talk about Israel and AIPAC, with increasingly open criticism of the Israeli government’s actions , some Jewish Democrats and Republicans responded with charges of antisemitism — and some Republicans started leaning into overt Islamophobia , particularly in Michigan . In turn, Republicans made bold predictions that Democrats would see a large drop in support this year, especially in Michigan (with an anti-Israel Senate candidate ) and New York , where they counted on Jewish voters to rally to the more pro-Israel party.

In the end, there was no mass exodus of Jewish voters — but the exit polls did report a slight shift toward the GOP this year: 68-31, compared to 78-22 in 2024. Other post-election surveys show similar dynamics. (The numbers can vary, in part because different pollsters use different metrics for measuring Jewish support and identity, and also because exit polls can be imprecise.) The Jewish Electorate Institute’s polling from the Mellman Group , for example, shows that while Democrats still held a large, 44-point advantage at the end of the day, (69 percent to the 25 percent that backed the GOP) that was smaller than the margin in 2024, and nearly 20 points smaller than their margin in 2018’s blue wave. That’s an anomaly, given the scale of the tsunami this year.

Even the most Democratic-friendly poll, from GBAO Strategies, had a kind of rightward signal, though a longer-horizon one: It showed nearly identical levels of Democratic support among Jewish voters this year as in 2024 — but both those figures, about 70 percent, are lower than Jewish Democratic support in 2022 (74 percent) and 2020 (77 percent), noted The Forward .

This shift away from Democrats looked especially dramatic in Michigan, where The Forward also noted last week that the winning Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed underperformed other Democratic candidates in precincts with large Jewish populations. In another piece of data, a Michigan exit poll from the NORC-Civic Health and Elections Project, there was a more dramatic result, albeit with a tiny sample size of about 100 people: Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers winning a majority of Jewish voters, 52-47 , a much worse result than it found for House Democratic candidates, who won the demographic by more than 30 points . Though small, it adds to other evidence of Democratic underperformance with Jewish voters in the Senate contest.

In surveys about their views, Jewish voters are sending signals that should put both parties on notice. A quarter of Republican Jews in the Mellman Group’s poll reported being concerned their party is “too accepting of antisemitic rhetoric within the Party” while a third said it’s “becoming too much of a home for White nationalists and the far right.”

More than a third of Jewish Democrats, similarly, said they worry the party is becoming “too accepting of antisemitic rhetoric within the Party,” while a quarter think it’s “becoming too much of a home for socialists and the far left.” Given how much larger the Jewish Democratic base is than the Republican one, and how central it is to winning coalitions in battlegrounds, these concerns pose a bigger electoral risk for the Democrats, particularly if the anti-Israel left grows into an even larger and more vocal wing of the party.
Protestants, and evangelicals, showed weaker Republican support
When it comes to evangelical Christians, the data suggests there was a different change afoot in the electorate.

They are perhaps the most important, or at least influential, religious group in American politics, given their strong and stable support for the Republican Party for the last 50 years. That loyalty has delivered them tremendous influence within party politics, while Trump, in particular, seems to have had a unique ability to turn these voters out during presidential elections. And at least in this year’s elections, that level of support for the GOP did not drop: they backed Republicans 82-16 , consistent with their support for Trump in 2024 .
What they didn’t do in 2026 is show up.

Exit polls suggest they made up a smaller share of the electorate when compared to 2026. That suggests a combination of lower turnout and lower enthusiasm may have contributed to Republican losses — even if those who did vote remained firmly Republican.

Still, the national results obscure one other notable trend that Burge, the religion scholar, noted from the 10 congressional districts with the highest share of evangelical voters — notably concentrated in the South (Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Tennessee). Each of these districts swung left, by an average of 23 points — more than in Catholic or nonevangelical mainline Protestant districts. This suggests stronger turnout and enthusiasm from the non-evangelical portion of these local electorates, which skews more Democratic — and in turn a weaker ability by Republican candidates to turn out evangelical voters in the way that Trump seems like he uniquely can.

In sharp contrast to evangelicals, the oldest but least-healthy strain of American Christianity — the mainline Protestant denominations like Episcopalians, Presbyterians, and Methodists — seems to have delivered a more politically interesting result this year. Many of the House and Senate seats that flipped for the Democrats this year were won by mainline Protestants in Iowa, Kansas, and Texas. They represent what used to be the dominant Christian electorate — which this year demonstrated it could still be a decisive part of a winning Democratic majority.

Heavily mainline districts swung by an average of 15 points toward Democrats, and each of the top eight districts ended up flipping to the Democratic column. The exit polls showed a Democratic gain among Protestants and nonevangelical Christians in general — moving from backing Republicans 63-36 in 2024 to 60-39 this year , a 6-point swing on the margins that can explain these flips.

As these numbers suggest, this is a demographic that seems more ripe for moderate Democratic appeals in the future — though they have been neglected by the establishment left over the last few decades.

We have less data and reliable post-election polling so far on what happened with other parts of the electorate, like Muslim voters, Hindus, and Mormons. What data we do have suggests they all played a part in forming the tidal wave that carried Democrats to their stunning victory last week. But above it all, this year’s results suggest that religious voters can function as swing voters in the post-Trump future, play an influential role in forming winning coalitions, and are not solely the domain of the Republican Party.

articles.headline: After Giving Away Thousands of Dollars in Cosmetics, Fortnite is Teasing a Big Reveal For Captain X, Its Mysterious Masked Treasure Man — With Fan Guesses Ranging From Mr Beast to Obama
keyFacts: Fortnite is teasing the identity reveal of the masked character Captain X during a live event on December 5.
Captain X recently appeared at the Streamer Awards 2026 to confirm the upcoming unmasking date.
Fans are speculating that the character might be portrayed by a celebrity or internet personality like MrBeast.
body: Fortnite is teasing a big reveal for its upcoming December 5 live event, which will reveal the identity of mysterious new character Captain X.

The game has previously employed big-name stars such as Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson and Brie Larson to portray notable in-game characters, and appears to be on the cusp of unveiling yet another casting of some significance.

Captain X made their debut at the beginning of Fortnite's current treasure-hunting mini-season, though their motives are currently unclear. As Fortnite's heroes hunt a fresh macguffin, Captain X has seemingly allowed them to make steady progress, while the game's story has suggested the character could also simply be letting players do their legwork instead, before swooping in to steal the prize.

At the same time, Fortnite itself has introduced a treasure hunting mechanic where players can win a fortnight of free access to the game's lucrative Item Shop — something that has sent concurrent player numbers soaring into the millions (all timed to cushion the blow of GTA 6's launch.)

Whether Captain X turns out to be friend or foe remains unclear, as does their relation to the game's wider storyline. This currently features a roster of surviving heroes from much of the game's past decade returning to face down Geno, Fortnite's uber Big Bad from the days when Epic Games' former creative boss Donald Mustard was still in charge of the storyline.
Should Geno actually be defeated, finally, will Captain X be revealed as the next major threat? Or perhaps they will be a new hero for players to follow, should Jonesy finally fall in battle?

Whatever is the case, Epic Games is clearly now teasing that there's more to Captain X than meets the eye. Last night at the Streamer Awards 2026, Captain X turned up in person wearing a mask to deliver a hand-written note confirming that they would be fully unveiled on December 5 — the date of Fortnite's next Chapter-ending live event.

Genuine question. Who could this possibly be that would be both exciting to see and fitting for Captain X's character. Like, the Foundation being The Rock only worked because there was a year of buildup and a lack of notable names in Fortnite. We have like everyone in the game now.
Not even trying to be miserable or anything here, I'm just absolutely lost as to who he(?) could possibly be.
— kat (@kattylotl) November 13, 2026

Currently, Captain X has only appeared in-game with their face covered, while their dialogue has been disguised with a heavy voice filter. (Players previously worked out that The Rock was playing a key character pretty quickly from his voice lines, even though he remained masked for almost a year — something that has not yet happened this time around.)

But who is it under the mask? Fans are speculating that the character will be played by a well-known actor or celebrity, with many suspecting that MrBeast has been brought on board. The YouTube star is already available in Fortnite as a character skin, and Captain X's ability to dole out hugely valuable prizes certainly lines up with MrBeast's usual shtick. Other fans have suggested the X is actually a clue this will be a new character played by Elon Musk, which seems extremely unlikely. And even less possibly, others have rounded on the idea that this seemingly generous person is actually President Barack Obama — which would certainly be a booking.
If you can tear yourself away from GTA 6 in time for December's Fortnite live event, we'll find out for sure what's going on, in just under a month's time.

articles.headline: Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration
keyFacts: Germany coach Jürgen Klopp said Felix Nmecha agreed not to repeat his controversial goal celebration linked to a group accused of discrimination.
Klopp stated Nmecha assured him that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone.
Germany will play Serbia on Friday aiming to keep alive their chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals.
body: With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.
Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.
This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.
Nmecha 'does not discriminate against anyone'
Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.
"Last weekend I saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.
"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."
He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.
Nations League quarterfinal berth up for grabs

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.
"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.
Just 5,000 children and coaches to attend

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.
"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

articles.headline: Whoop Humans is a social network designed for fitness enthusiasts
keyFacts: Whoop has launched Whoop Humans, a social network for users to share verified exercise data from their screenless wearable trackers.
Users can follow friends, comment on posts, share workout photos, and adjust their data privacy settings at any time.
Whoop Humans is currently live and accessible to members through the company's official app.
body: Whoop Humans is a social network designed for fitness enthusiasts
Members can only share data from their Whoop wearables as guarantee of authenticity.

Whoop, the company behind the popular screenless wearable trackers, has launched a social network for users who like sharing their exercise details and fitness efforts called Whoop Humans. It's a rather unusual name, so you might be wondering how the company decided on it. Well, Will Ahmed, the CEO of Whoop, described it as the "most verifiably human network ever launched." Members can share their fitness data on the social network, including their sleep, recovery, strain and activities information. In all cases, the data comes from a Whoop wearable. That's "real-world information that cannot simply be generated as a conventional text post" at a time when "traditional social networks are increasingly filled with artificial content," the company said in its announcement.

Whoop already has Teams, which connects users through groups and leaderboards. But the new social network lets users follow friends and family directly to comment and react to their posts. The company envisions a social network, wherein people can check in on each other based on their progress. The idea is for members to be able to congratulate each other when they reach their goals or to be able to remind a friend to take it easy if they see the other's "Recovery" data is low. Hard to imagine most people taking an interest in another's fitness information, but people who are very much into fitness might see value in the social network.

In addition to being able to share fitness data, members will also be able to share photos from their workouts with a feature called "Moments." They can keep those Moments private, however, and, thankfully, they can choose which workout types or achievements appear on the social network. Just because they're wearing a Whoop doesn't mean their data will automatically be shared. Members can still update their sharing preferences any time they want. Whoop Humans is now live and available through the company's app.

articles.headline: Stephen A Smith debriefs interview with President Trump, warns Democrats face steep challenge
keyFacts: ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith debriefed his interview with President Donald Trump on Fox News, discussing midterm GOP losses.
Smith said Trump refused to take blame for midterm losses, attributing the defeats to weak Republican candidates rather than his presidency.
Smith cautioned that the Democratic Party faces steep challenges due to internal division caused by its progressive far-left flank.
body: Stephen A Smith debriefs interview with President Trump, warns Democrats face steep challenge
By
Nora Moriarty , Fox News
Published Nov. 13, 2026, 3:21 a.m. ET
See more of our coverage in your search results.

ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith debriefed his White House interview with President Donald Trump during an appearance Thursday on “Hannity” and cautioned Democrats over the influence of the party’s far-left flank.
Smith said the pair discussed “devastating” GOP midterm losses during a 40-minute, wide-ranging interview and criticized Trump for refusing to take blame, saying he was “immovable” on that point.
“We talked about the devastating losses in the midterms and how the GOP essentially got slaughtered,” Smith told Fox News host Sean Hannity.
“I asked him, is he willing to point the finger at himself, and he was dogged… he was immovable in that regard,” he added.

Trump repeatedly told Americans during his midterm blitz to vote as if he were on the ballot, but Smith said the commander-in-chief removed himself from that narrative during their Thursday interview.

“He said, ‘I wasn’t on the ballot.’ I said, ‘That makes absolutely no sense, Mr. President. You said, put you on a ballot. That’s what you told the American people to do.’ He said, ‘Well, they didn’t do it.’ I said, ‘Well, what if they did do it and that was the reason you lost,’” Smith explained.
“He refused to accept that,” he continued. “His attitude is that the candidates were not that great. If it were him that was running, this would not have happened. That’s his mentality.”
Smith explained why he doesn’t agree with Trump’s perception of how the midterms played out and argued that the blue wave stems from Americans being dissatisfied with his presidency.
“I think that he is somebody that is convinced his way is what it is. I just don’t agree with him,” Smith said.
“I think the American people made a statement against what they were seeing from him in terms of him not having his eye on the ball and coming across as a bit detached in their eyes,” he added.

Smith told Fox News that Trump also gave him pushback when discussing the impact of the Iran War and tariffs on voter sentiment and the economy. He also addressed speculation that Trump offered him the role of White House press secretary.
“That was absolutely hilarious,” Smith said. “Evidently, they don’t know about the life that I live and the kind of affluence that ESPN and Disney have blessed me with.”
“I wouldn’t take that pay cut for almost anything but the presidency,” he continued. “That ain’t happening. Press secretary? Please.”
Smith, who has lodged criticism at both Democrats and Republicans, warned that the Democratic Party faces a challenge from its far-left side.

“I definitely think that right now, the Democrats have a challenge on their hands because clearly there’s a lot of people out there that view the Democratic Party as a divided party,” he said. “Now they will tell you they’re a very big tent and there’s room for everybody, but I think that the progressive left has shown you there isn’t room for everybody.”
“If you’re not willing to capitulate to their desires, their wishes and their ideological beliefs 100%, then they got a problem with you,” he added.
Smith called out Democrats who have declined interviews and expressed gratitude that Trump agreed to sit down with him for an interview.

“[Trump] was just very rigid and immovable in his thinking that it was blown by the people who lost and that the candidates on the Republican side simply were not good enough. It was not about him,” Smith said.
“… I give him credit,” he continued. “I asked a question, and he answered, and he didn’t run from anything.”

articles.headline: After Jensen Huang, Big Tech Has a Chance to Learn From Nvidia’s Mistakes
keyFacts: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following allegations of extramarital affairs involving a company employee and an alleged Chinese spy.
Panelists at Web Summit said Nvidia's crisis highlights the dangers of allowing tech CEOs to wield unchecked power without board oversight.
Nvidia named Collette Kress as interim CEO and announced it is appointing its first chairman for its board.
body: What now for Nvidia? This was the question on everyone’s lips at the illustrious Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon on Thursday in the hours after CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation.

Huang’s departure followed a series of allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an Nvidia employee and one with a woman who has been identified as a possible Chinese spy. The company, whose computer chips are at the core of generative AI’s disruptive powers, is valued at around $4 trillion, making it one of the most valuable in the world. A co-founder, Huang has been with Nvidia since its earliest days three decades ago, making it hard to imagine the company without him at the helm.

There’s nothing quite like a salacious, market-moving scandal to create a buzz at a tech event. The Web Summit organizers leaned into the news, quickly assembling a panel of tech experts to discuss whether Nvidia was bigger than its CEO.
More from CNET

Nothing in the allegations changes the fact that Huang is probably the godfather of the AI revolution, said investor and financial writer Adam Kobeissi. “He was the central figure,” Kobeissi said, even if he wasn’t the only person responsible for Nvidia’s success.
“This company is going to survive and thrive with or without him,” he added. “I don’t think this is some sort of bubble-popping moment where everything comes crumbling down.”

Sweeping financial investments and expectations across the AI industry have driven stock prices and company valuations to dizzying heights, with many critics warning of a bubble just waiting to burst with destabilizing effects. As powerful as Nvidia has become, it could be caught in the center of such a maelstrom.
While such a concentration of power is not the way to create resilient companies, said Ryan LaSalle, CEO of cybersecurity company Nisos, like Kobeissi he thinks Nvidia will weather the storm.

Interim Nvidia CEO Collette Kress, who has been with the company since 2013, is known for having a ton of loyalty within Nvidia, he said. “In a company of that much brainpower, there will be some natural leaders who can help shepherd them to the next chapter.”
Great power and no responsibility
One big question put to panel participants was whether Nvidia’s board made a mistake allowing one person to have so much power.
It wasn’t just a mistake of corporate culture, said Carissa Veliz, associate professor of philosophy at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI. It was also a mistake in terms of democracy.

For one person to wield so much power over decisions affecting the economy and national security means something has gone wrong and has revealed how vulnerable we are, Veliz said. If we look at the history of corporations, she said, there used to be a tradition of proving to the government that you were doing good for your country to earn your right to exist and get certain tax breaks.

“At the moment, we have shifted from that kind of framework to a framework in which a corporation is allowed to be essentially a kind of psychopath that only cares about its own profits, that only has duties to shareholders and which can be structured in any way, including a very powerful CEO with very little oversight,” she said.

Gil Duran, author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, said that he thought Nvidia’s errors in the lead-up to this moment would be studied in business and public relations crisis management classes.

“The board was completely missing out on most of the truth and the facts,” he said, referencing news reports that said Huang a year ago hired a law firm known for covering up sex scandals and President Donald Trump in May had been told about the CEO’s affair with the alleged Chinese spy.
“I don’t think there’s any other way to look at it but a catastrophe,” he said.
An end to the era of ‘small king’ CEOs?
Duran and Veliz agreed that it was time to ensure tech CEOs face real oversight.
“These guys face no accountability and no supervision, and that’s part of the problem,” said Veliz. “These kind of small kings have their own small kingdoms… and they get away with almost anything.”
CEOs like Elon Musk at SpaceX and Sam Altman at OpenAI have enormous influence not only in their own companies but also across the national economy.

What we’re seeing in Huang’s downfall is the shattering of a myth about genius founders, said Duran. He questioned whether it would spark actual change, however, given that the market’s addiction to the narrative of great, powerful founders.
“The fact that they can just tumble markets with their personal lives that become geopolitical crises – this is an insane amount of power to outsource,” he said.

If we can tone down the myth, this moment provides a chance to look at where we’ve gone wrong and do better, Veliz said. There’s opportunity here, she added – to raise up companies that can build the kinds of technology we need, support democracies rather than erode them, aren’t based on surveillance and prediction, and can behave transparently.
Lessons from a scandal
For every other tech behemoth out there, there is plenty to be learned from Huang’s downfall. The concentration of power in one individual is not, as LaSalle pointed out, a safe long-term strategy.
What’s needed is more oversight and accountability from a company’s board of directors. In announcing Huang’s resignation, Nvidia also said it was appointing its first chairman for its board.

Huang’s entanglement with a potential honeypot is also an opportunity for tech companies to think about security, said LaSalle. No matter how sophisticated cybersecurity threats are becoming in the age of AI, he added, “people are still the simplest way in.”

Duran warned about the potential damage ahead if we fail to seize this as a moment to change. “If you look at the AI CEO vision of the future, it’s massive economic destruction so that a handful of people can become trillionaires,” he said. “No one voted for that. Nobody wants that, and we have a short window of time to collapse it before they collapse us.”
Disclosure: Katie Collins traveled to Lisbon as a guest of Web Summit to serve as a panel moderator. Her reporting from the event was independent of that role.

articles.headline: Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang’s ‘scheme’ with Trump
keyFacts: Congressional Democrats launched an inquiry on Thursday into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia chip sales to China.
Democrats wrote a letter questioning Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick regarding an alleged illegal revenue-sharing scheme and Nvidia donations to Trump projects.
Nvidia ousted CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday after he confessed to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
body: Democrats on Thursday opened an inquiry into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China. Earlier on Thursday, the company ousted its CEO Jensen Huang. He also agreed to testify to a different set of Republican-led Congressional committees.

Huang was removed from the company he founded after he confessed to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. (He has since been accused of having more affairs, with Nvidia employees.)

The alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Democratic inquiry comes from Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. As the minority party, they can ask questions but can’t compel answers.
Their humdinger of a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asks the department to preserve records about an arrangement they find questionable and, they allege, illegal.

“The scheme worked like this,” as the letter describes it. President Trump agreed to sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China as long as the chips, manufactured by Taiwan, were first shipped to the United States. On arriving, Trump added a tariff “effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system,” the letter said. Then the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, issued an export license.

By the way, the deal between Trump and Nvidia to share revenue was public. In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD both agreed to share 15% of their revenue from chip sales to China with the U.S. government as part of a deal to secure export licenses, the AP reported at the time.

But the letter questions why Lutnick continued to allow Megaspeed to buy chips even after he was reportedly informed by U.S. intelligence of their suspicions of Alice Huang and of Jensen Huang’s relationship with her. It questions why the department reportedly green-lit other Asian companies to buy Nvidia chips “with no physical presence at their listed addresses.” So the inquiry is aimed at the administration, not just at Nvidia and Huang.

The letter also questions how Nvidia’s donations to Trump’s projects factored in. It notes that the export deal was approved after Trump learned of “Mr. Huang’s compromised position” in sleeping with an alleged spy, and after Nvidia donated $26 million toward Trump’s projects, including the ballroom. It appears to be asking if Trump used his knowledge of the affair to secure donations from Nvidia.

Interestingly, in a “60 Minutes” interview with President Trump that aired on Sunday, Trump mentioned how he and his team had threatened an unnamed AI exec with jail, and after that, the exec “totally changed.”

This Congressional investigation into Nvidia’s China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke. The Republican-led group involves leaders from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House Intelligence Committee. That group has demanded that Huang come to them and testify in a closed-door session. They had threatened to subpoena him if he didn’t voluntarily agree. On Thursday, after his resignation, he agreed.

articles.headline: Rep.-Elect Don Leonard Says Fellow Dems Threatened Him Over Hakeem Jeffries Vote
keyFacts: Rep.-elect Don Leonard stated that senior Democrats threatened him with political retaliation if he did not unconditionally support Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker.
Leonard said the threats included making his time in Washington difficult and ensuring he loses his election in two years.
Leonard conditioned his support for Jeffries on ending U.S. support for the war in Iran and Israel.
body: A newly elected House member who flipped a district seat blue in Ohio said he was threatened by senior Democrats if he didn’t unconditionally support Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) for House speaker.
Jeffries, now the minority leader, is the likely choice to succeed Rep. Mike Johnson (R-La.) after a blue midterm wave delivered the House and Senate to the Democrats.
But Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) didn’t appear to be feeling the collegial vibe this week during orientation on Capitol Hill.

Leonard said fellow lawmakers “told me in no uncertain terms that the decision as to whether or not I support Jeffries ... would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next two years here in Washington as well as being sure to lose my election in two years.”

“It’s part of the stuff you see in the movies,” he continued in a clip shared by HuffPost alum Ryan Grim of Drop Site News. “It’s a whole other thing when, you know, when it’s in person by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you but expect you to wear the team jersey and be a good team player.”
Leonard said his conditions to back Jeffries included “ending U.S. support for the war in Iran and the country, Israel, that led us into it.”

“It was so much less cinematic. It was actually a dinner with senior elected officials, and I let them know where my position was on the speaker, and they were offering very friendly advice with very stark consequences,” Leonard said.
“Welcome to Washington, D.C., right? I’m not shocked, but I’m disappointed,” Leonard replied.
